Key Summary Points Why carry out this study? The phase 3 SURMOUNT-J clinical trial demonstrated that Japanese adults with obesity disease achieved clinically meaningful body weight loss through the administration of tirzepatide for 72 weeks. This study aimed to explore participants’ experiences with tirzepatide during SURMOUNT-J, as well as body weight changes, other weight loss treatments, and body weight management after the trial. What was learned from the study? Participants reported that changes in eating behaviors acquired during SURMOUNT-J were retained after stopping tirzepatide but not changes in exercise behaviors; approximately three-quarters of participants expressed a desire to continue drug therapy for obesity disease treatment. Providing information to people with obesity disease and connecting them with appropriate medical interventions are essential. Introduction Obesity-related health disorders (e.g., hypertension, dyslipidemia, glucose tolerance disorder) often occur at a lower body mass index (BMI) in Japanese people than those from Western countries (≥ 25 kg/m 2 vs. ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ) [ 1 ]. On the basis of this, the Japan Society for the Study of Obesity have advocated the concept of “obesity disease,” which uses a BMI threshold of ≥ 25 kg/m 2 to define obesity disease, rather than the ≥ 30 kg/m 2 threshold for obesity used in the rest of the world [ 1 , 2 ]. People with a high BMI (≥ 25 kg/m 2 ) and with either certain obesity-related health disorders or an accumulation of visceral fat are diagnosed with obesity disease in Japan [ 1 , 3 , 4 ]. The diagnostic criteria comprise 11 obesity-related health disorders, including glucose tolerance disorders (type 2 diabetes and impaired glucose tolerance), dyslipidemia, and hypertension [ 1 ], all of which are associated with an increased incidence of cardiometabolic disease and an increased risk of premature death [ 5 – 8 ]. Obesity disease is also associated with an increased risk of several cancers and has been identified as a public health concern [ 9 ]. The global prevalence of obesity (defined as a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ) among adults was 16% in 2022 [ 10 ]. The prevalence varies by geographical region, with the Americas and Europe having the highest rates [ 11 ]. The number of adults living with obesity is expected to further increase over time [ 12 ]. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), which increases the risk of liver-related and cardiovascular-related morbidity and mortality, is relatively common in people with obesity, and studies have shown that body weight loss can improve markers of liver disease in patients with the condition [ 13 ]. Among adults in Japan, 31.5% of men and 21.1% of women have a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m 2 [ 14 ]; the proportion of people with a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m 2 has been trending upward since the 1970s [ 15 , 16 ]. Obesity disease-related cardiovascular risk factors can be reduced with a loss of 5–10% of body weight through lifestyle approaches such as caloric restriction, increased physical activity, and behavioral therapy [ 17 , 18 ]. Such approaches may also improve health-related quality of life [ 19 ]. Unfortunately, lifestyle approaches alone fail to achieve sustainable body weight loss in most individuals with obesity disease [ 20 ]. Pharmacological interventions are available for people with obesity disease; however, they are only indicated in people for whom changes in diet, exercise, and behavioral therapy are inadequate [ 1 ]. Currently available pharmacotherapies include glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, which are used to treat diabetes and have been shown to reduce body weight [ 21 ]. Tirzepatide is a dual GLP-1 and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor agonist [ 22 ]. It is a once-weekly subcutaneous injectable drug that has been shown to induce substantial and sustained body weight loss in adults with obesity or overweight [ 23 ]. The SURMOUNT-J clinical trial (SURMOUNT-J) was a phase 3 trial of the efficacy and safety of tirzepatide (10 mg or 15 mg) versus placebo on a background of a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity in Japanese adults with obesity disease [ 24 ]. The trial demonstrated a clinically meaningful body weight loss with once-weekly tirzepatide for 72 weeks [ 24 ]. Over 94% of participants who received tirzepatide achieved ≥ 5% body weight reduction and over half achieved ≥ 20% body weight reduction from baseline to week 72. There were also improvements in body composition, metabolic and glycemic parameters, obesity-related health disorders, hepatic factors, cardiometabolic risk factors, and patient-reported outcomes with tirzepatide treatment. While SURMOUNT-J provided quantitative data demonstrating the efficacy, safety, and patient-reported outcomes of tirzepatide, qualitative assessments of participants’ subjective experiences during and after the trial have not been performed. The primary objective of the present study was to explore participant experiences with tirzepatide as a treatment for obesity disease in SURMOUNT-J and body weight changes after the trial [ 24 ]. Secondary objectives were to explore participant experiences with both other treatments and body weight management after SURMOUNT-J, and to understand what healthcare provider support participants desire for their treatment of obesity disease. While a similar study was conducted with participants in the SURMOUNT-4 clinical trial in the USA [ 25 ], the present study represents the first such study in the Japanese population. Methods Study Design and Setting This was a cross-sectional, non-interventional, semi-structured, qualitative exit interview study conducted in Japan from August 2024 through October 2024. Patients who were assigned to the tirzepatide treatment group in SURMOUNT-J were identified by the principal investigators at each study site using patient medical records [ 24 ]. Potential participants were then recruited to the present study at outpatient visits, by email or messenger applications (e.g., LINE smartphone app), or by telephone. Each potential participant was provided with a two-dimensional code to initiate their participation in the study. After participants were recruited to the study and responded to screening questions, they were asked to provide electronic informed consent. Physicians confirmed participant eligibility based on the information in their medical records and their responses to the screening questions. Before the interview was conducted, participants completed a questionnaire, in which they provided information related to body weight, treatment history of obesity disease, and their participation in clinical trials other than SURMOUNT-J. Additionally, they completed a pre-survey (Supplementary Fig. S1 ), which was not for collecting data but rather served to provide information on each participant’s journey to support the interview process. The pre-survey was designed to take approximately 20 min to complete and was conducted to mitigate recall bias. Other background data were collected from each participant’s medical record. Participants then scheduled an online interview (Supplementary Text S1 ), which was expected to take approximately 60 min to complete and was conducted using a web-based conferencing system. Interviews were conducted by an experienced interviewer who was not an author of the present manuscript, was female, and was a moderator and medical writer at the time the study was conducted. She did not have any prior relationship with the study participants and had performed 420 medical-related interviews since 2020, 40 of which were related to obesity or lifestyle disease. The participants did not have any prior knowledge of the interviewer. All interviews were recorded and transcribed by 3H (3H Clinical Trial Inc., Tokyo, Japan). The transcripts were not returned to the participants for comment or correction. The interviews included five sections, with each section comprising two to five main questions and taking 5–15 min to complete. Anonymized data and interview transcripts were provided to Mebix Inc. (Tokyo, Japan), which performed qualitative analysis of the information. Three coders participated in the analysis. Participants did not provide feedback on the study findings. The study was reported in accordance with the COREQ guidelines. Participants Although six study sites were initially scheduled to participate, one study site was excluded because of a regulatory non-compliance issue, resulting in five study sites being included in this interview study. Participants who met the following inclusion criteria were eligible for enrollment: assigned to the active treatment group in SURMOUNT-J, and completed the 72-week SURMOUNT-J study ( N = 125), and were within 24 months of completing the active drug group requirements in SURMOUNT-J [ 24 ]. Participants were excluded from the study if they met any of the following exclusion criteria: history of malignancy or thyroid disease between the end of SURMOUNT-J and their participation in the study pre-survey, or used tirzepatide after completion of SURMOUNT-J. The study protocol was approved by the Takahashi Clinic Ethics Committee (LNW00210); this approval covered the necessary ethics approvals for all five study sites. The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles described in the Declaration of Helsinki, the Ethical Guidelines for Medical and Biological Research Involving Human Subjects, and all applicable Japanese laws and regulations. All participants provided electronic informed consent to participate in the study and to publish the verbatim responses from the study. SURMOUNT-J [ 24 ] is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT04844918 ). Data Collection Participant background data at the time of enrollment in SURMOUNT-J, as well as body weight following completion of SURMOUNT-J, were collected from study site medical records and transcribed to the electronic data capture system of SURMOUNT-J [ 24 ]. Background data (body weight, treatment history of obesity disease, and information about participation in clinical trials other than SURMOUNT-J) at the time of enrollment in the present study were self-reported by participants. Participant interviews were conducted to collect information related to the following topics: experience related to tirzepatide treatment during SURMOUNT-J, experience with other treatments and body weight management after completion of SURMOUNT-J, experience with body weight change after SURMOUNT-J, healthcare provider support sought by participants, and the psychological burden experienced with tirzepatide injections. Participant narratives included in the text and Supplementary File 3 are not comprehensive but provide narratives that are representative of each interview section. Data Analysis The target sample size was set to 30 participants, based on the number of participants in SURMOUNT-J [ 24 ] who were able to access the present study. Categorical variables are summarized using frequency and proportion, while continuous variables are summarized with descriptive statistics. Content analysis was conducted on the interview data and transcripts using NVivo software (QSR International Pty Ltd., Doncaster, Australia). The analysis was conducted in an inductive manner. To enhance the credibility of the qualitative findings, the analyses were conducted using triangulation, where a researcher other than the analyst or a third party confirmed the interpretation of results. A coding tree was also created in NVivo software to ensure transparency in the analysis process. Discrepancies among the three coders were resolved through discussion and consensus. Sex/gender analysis was not conducted as qualitative research typically involves small sample sizes, making analysis by sex/gender prone to overgeneralization. Furthermore, this study aimed to understand how participants interpret their experiences as a whole; thus, it focused on common patterns rather than differences by sex or gender. Results Participants Thirty-two individuals provided informed consent to participate in the study. Of those, one participant withdrew consent, and two participants were lost to follow-up. In total, 29 participants completed the interviews, which represented 23.2% of patients in the active treatment group ( N = 125) of SURMOUNT-J. Participant background characteristics are shown in Table 1 . At SURMOUNT-J enrollment, the mean ± standard deviation (SD) age and body weight among the 29 participants were 45.8 ± 9.8 years and 92.1 ± 15.8 kg, respectively. The mean ± SD body weight was 76.8 ± 16.7 kg at the end of the trial and 84.4 ± 19.2 kg at the time of enrollment in the present study. The most common obesity-related health issues were dyslipidemia (93.1%), hypertension (48.3%), hyperuricemia and/or gout (34.5%), and NAFLD (31.0%). Most participants (75.9%) did not participate in another clinical trial after completing SURMOUNT-J. The mean ± SD (range, interquartile range) number of days from the last tirzepatide dose to the study interview was 617.8 ± 59.6 (507–715, 577.0–683.0) days and there was a mean ± SD weight change of 7.59 ± 6.65 kg from the end of SURMOUNT-J to enrollment in the present study. SURMOUNT-J concluded in June 2023, and the first participant was enrolled in the present study in August 2024. Most participants reported that the device was convenient and easy to use and that resistance to injection was quickly resolved (72.4% for each). Over half of the participants reported that they had difficulties with the refrigeration and transport of the device (69.0%). Just under half of participants reported that the dosing frequency was convenient (44.8%), and approximately one-third reported that handling the cap was inconvenient (31.0%). Obesity Awareness Participants provided reasons why they perceived obesity as a disease. These included a psychological problem causing an uncontrollable appetite (24.1%), an improvement in body weight and laboratory data post-treatment (10.3%), and an increase in the risk of other diseases (3.4%). Participants also commented on why they did not perceive obesity as a disease. These included constitution (20.7%), the absence of other diseases (10.3%), and the potential for body weight loss with effort (6.9%). Discussion Most study participants experienced body weight loss and improved appetite control during SURMOUNT-J. The use of tirzepatide was predominantly associated with changes in eating habits, but there was less influence on changes in exercise habits. Overall, 75.9% of participants expressed a willingness to continue drug therapy. Changes in eating behaviors that were initiated during the trial were maintained by just over half of the participants after the trial ended. The interviews provided some insights on obesity management needs according to the study participants, including potential unmet needs for personalized diet and exercise therapy, and improved information on obesity-related risks and departments that offer obesity treatment. Regarding transferability, the characteristics of the participants in SURMOUNT-J were nearly identical in terms of age, sex ratio, and mean body weight at enrollment to the characteristics of the participants in the present study [ 24 ]. This suggests similarity between participants in this study and those in SURMOUNT-J for these particular variables. Participants reported changes in their eating habits during SURMOUNT-J. These changes included a loss of appetite because of tirzepatide, changes in food preferences, an intentional increase in the amount of vegetables eaten, and the selection of meals according to a calorie table. After the trial ended, 51.7% of participants maintained the changes in eating behavior that were initiated during the trial. This included a change in their sense of taste and a lack of desire for greasy foods, suggesting that some medications can trigger changes in eating habits. Studies of other body weight loss drugs, such as semaglutide, also have been reported to change eating habits, including fewer food cravings, better eating control/less emotional eating, and changes in food preference [ 26 , 27 ]. In the present study, a small proportion of participants (10.3%) reported that they no longer experienced joy when eating during the trial, which could potentially have a negative impact on their quality of life. Some participants reported lighter body movements (51.7%) and changes in exercise habits (37.9%) during the trial. When undertaking activities of daily life such as climbing stairs, these participants noticed that their body felt lighter and that they felt less fatigued. Such experiences were considered to be very beneficial. Importantly, while some participants (37.9%) reported changes to their exercise habits during the trial, 44.8% said that they were unable to maintain exercise habits after the trial ended. The use of tirzepatide appears to be associated with changes in eating habits rather than changes in exercise habits, indicating that it may be difficult to induce behavioral changes in exercise. Many participants thought that general guidance on exercise was not useful for them and expressed their preference for individualized guidance. This may reflect a potential unmet need for healthcare providers to prescribe exercise therapy at medical facilities. Some participants were not able to maintain their body weight loss after the trial ended and experienced a rebound in their body weight. Some participants (13.8%) relied on alternative methods, such as esthetic treatments, to try to prevent regaining the body weight lost during the trial. Some participants also considered obesity treatment as a beauty treatment. The difficulty that some participants experienced in maintaining body weight loss after the trial ended highlights the importance of recognizing obesity as a disease and providing patients with the appropriate treatment. Some participants reported seeking information on places where they could receive obesity treatment and the need to be provided with information regarding obesity-related risks. This suggests that there is room for improvement in the information provided by healthcare providers to patients about obesity and the associated risks, as well as treatment options [ 28 ]. While many participants had no concerns about entering a facility called “Obesity Clinic,” some did. Thus, when naming departments or clinics, it may be beneficial to consider names that reduce stigma, are accessible, avoid patient discomfort and self-consciousness, and do not cause psychological hesitance [ 29 ]. It is also important to raise awareness in society about obesity so that patients undergoing treatment for the disease do not feel stigmatized. The interviews revealed interesting insights on participant-preferred communication with and monitoring by healthcare providers. Some participants hoped their healthcare providers would manage the safety of their treatment and clinical data. Some participants were concerned with excessive body weight loss and wanted a healthcare provider to check whether their body weight loss was occurring in a safe and healthy manner. Although they had a positive view of body weight loss, some participants had anxiety around major changes they experienced with body weight loss, such as adverse reactions to treatment or unfavorable events caused by their body weight loss. These findings suggest that healthcare providers should always keep in mind the need to support patients, work to understand their patient’s feelings, and strive to provide effective communication and monitoring, thus potentially reducing patient anxiety. A patient experience study was conducted following the conclusion of SURMOUNT-4, a phase 3 trial of the efficacy and safety to tirzepatide in participants living with obesity or in those who were overweight with ≥ 1 weight-related comorbidity in the USA [ 25 ]. Similar findings between the SURMOUNT-4 exit interview study and the present study included the reported benefits during treatment (e.g., appetite decrease, increased positivity), that most participants wanted to continue tirzepatide (91% and 76%, respectively), and that most participants found the injection device easy to use (98% and 72%, respectively) [ 25 ]. Key differences were that the present study found that changes in dietary habits were maintained after discontinuing tirzepatide, but exercise habits were not. Additionally, the present study clarified the need for weight management after stopping tirzepatide treatment. Aspects regarding the post-discontinuation period, which were not investigated in the SURMOUNT-4 exit interview study, provided new insights from this study. This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. We did not use theoretical sampling, which assumes theoretical saturation. Rather, we used convenience sampling for participant recruitment. Thus, theoretical saturation could not be confirmed. The participants in the present study have some similar characteristics to those of SURMOUNT-J, but they are not representative of the participants in SURMOUNT-J in all aspects. It was assumed that participants would have a recall bias, so a pre-survey was conducted to encourage prior recall. Study participants were thought to be highly motivated to participate in clinical trials. As such, they may not be representative of people with obesity in the real-world environment. Additionally, the results may have been biased given that the present study only included participants who had completed tirzepatide treatment, meaning that those who discontinued treatment were not represented. Participants in this study were familiar with the Internet, suggesting the possibility of selection bias. During SURMOUNT-J, participants were advised to avoid leaving home as the clinical trial period overlapped with the COVID-19 pandemic. It is assumed that this resulted in the loss of opportunities to eat out and to exercise, which likely affected the diet and exercise regimen of participants during the trial. Finally, the sample size is small, and studies in larger populations will be of value. To gain a more holistic understanding of the patient experience with tirzepatide treatment, future studies are warranted to incorporate a comprehensive evaluation that includes not only positive experiences but also potential negative experiences and psychological outcomes. Furthermore, conducting studies with larger patient populations, including quantitative approaches, could allow for a more appropriate examination of the differences in treatment experiences between patients who maintained their post-treatment weight and those who regained weight. Conclusion This study used web-based interviews to explore participant experience both during and after SURMOUNT-J in which participants received tirzepatide treatment for 72 weeks. Participants who received tirzepatide treatment reported that they were able to maintain their changes in eating behavior but not exercise habits. Notably, three-quarters of participants expressed willingness to continue drug therapy for obesity disease treatment. This study highlights the importance of providing information to people with obesity disease and connecting them with appropriate medical interventions, including treatment. Why carry out this study?
The phase 3 SURMOUNT-J clinical trial demonstrated that Japanese adults with obesity disease achieved clinically meaningful body weight loss through the administration of tirzepatide for 72 weeks.
This study aimed to explore participants’ experiences with tirzepatide during SURMOUNT-J, as well as body weight changes, other weight loss treatments, and body weight management after the trial.
What was learned from the study?
Participants reported that changes in eating behaviors acquired during SURMOUNT-J were retained after stopping tirzepatide but not changes in exercise behaviors; approximately three-quarters of participants expressed a desire to continue drug therapy for obesity disease treatment.
Providing information to people with obesity disease and connecting them with appropriate medical interventions are essential.

1 INTRODUCTION Obesity is a multifaceted health condition associated with multiple complications, including an increased risk of chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes (T2D), cardiovascular disease, certain cancers and musculoskeletal disorders. Obesity can negatively impact mental health, leading to depression, anxiety and diminished quality of life (QOL). 1 While the World Health Organization (WHO) defines obesity as a body mass index (BMI) of ≥30 kg/m 2 , if the Working Group on Obesity in China definitions are applied (BMI ≥24 kg/m 2 for overweight; BMI ≥28 kg/m 2 for obesity), 1 , 2 China had the highest global prevalence of overweight or obesity in 2021, with roughly 50% of adults affected. This is projected to increase to two‐thirds of the adult population by 2030. 3 Pharmacological options for treating obesity in China are scarce; by 2023, only orlistat, beinaglutide and liraglutide were approved by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) of China for weight management. 4 , 5 , 6 As such, there is a strong unmet need for convenient medication for overweight and obesity in China. The efficacy and safety of once‐weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg, a glucagon‐like peptide‐1 receptor agonist (GLP‐1RA), have been demonstrated for weight management in the STEP programme. 7 Semaglutide 2.4 mg is approved for weight management in adults with obesity or overweight with ≥1 weight‐related comorbidity in the USA, Europe and other countries, including China (NMPA, June 2024). 8 , 9 , 10 In STEP 7 ( NCT04251156 ), efficacy and safety were demonstrated in a predominantly East Asian population with overweight or obesity, with or without T2D. 11 This prespecified analysis compared the efficacy and safety of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo as an adjunct to a reduced‐calorie diet and increased physical activity in Chinese participants enrolled in STEP 7. 2 MATERIALS AND METHODS 2.1 Trial design STEP 7 ( NCT04251156 ) was a phase 3a, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled, multicentre randomized trial (Figure S2 ). Full details of the trial design have been previously described. 11 This prespecified analysis of STEP 7 included a population of participants from mainland China (23 sites) and Hong Kong (one site). Briefly, eligible participants were aged ≥18 years with a history of ≥1 self‐reported unsuccessful dietary effort to lose weight, and a BMI of ≥30 kg/m 2 or ≥27 kg/m 2 with ≥1 of the following weight‐related comorbidities: hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiovascular disease, and T2D. Full eligibility criteria are in the supplementary materials ( p2 ). This study was conducted in accordance with the International Council for Harmonization of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use guidelines. 2.2 Procedures Participants were randomized 2:1 to receive either semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo, alongside a lifestyle intervention of approximately 500 kcal/day deficit in diet and 150 minutes/week of physical activity. Up to Week 16, participants followed a fixed‐dose escalation regimen for semaglutide with an initial dose of 0.25 mg, which was increased every 4 weeks to 0.5, 1.0, 1.7 and 2.4 mg/week. Participants then received a maintenance dose of semaglutide 2.4 mg until the end of treatment at 44 weeks. All participants provided written informed consent prior to trial‐related activities. 2.3 Outcomes The primary objective of this prespecified analysis was to compare the effect on body weight of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo in participants with overweight or obesity with or without T2D. The secondary objectives were to compare the effect of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo on cardiovascular risk factors, patient‐reported outcomes and glucose metabolism, and to assess safety and tolerability. All endpoints were assessed from baseline to Week 44. The primary endpoints were the percentage change in body weight and the proportion of participants who achieved ≥5% reduction in body weight. Confirmatory secondary endpoints were the proportion of participants who achieved ≥10% and ≥15% reduction in body weight, and changes in waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, Short Form‐36 v2 Health Survey acute version (SF‐36v2) physical functioning score and Impact of Weight on Quality of Life‐Lite Clinical Trials Version (IWQOL‐Lite‐CT) physical function score. Supportive secondary endpoints included the proportion of participants who achieved ≥20% reduction in body weight, and change in body weight, BMI, glycated haemoglobin (HbA 1c ) (with and without T2D), fasting plasma glucose (FPG), fasting serum insulin, diastolic blood pressure, lipids and fatty liver index (FLI) score (<30, ≥30, <60, ≥60). FLI was calculated using BMI, waist circumference, triglycerides and gamma‐glutamyl transferase levels. Change in body weight was additionally assessed according to participant baseline characteristic subgroups, including age, sex, weight, BMI, diabetes status and renal function. Safety endpoints reported until study end (Week 51) included the incidence of adverse events (AEs). Details of safety endpoints are included in the supplementary materials ( p4 ). 2.4 Statistical analysis This was a prespecified analysis of the STEP 7 trial, not included in the statistical testing hierarchy. As such, the superiority of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo cannot be ascertained in this population; however, statistical significance between groups could be determined. The following datasets were defined in the STEP 7 protocol and used in this prespecified analysis: the full analysis set, which included all randomized participants according to the intention‐to‐treat protocol, and the safety analysis set, which included all randomized participants exposed to at least one dose of the assigned randomized treatment. Two observation periods were defined: the in‐trial period was the uninterrupted time from randomization to the last interaction with the trial site or investigators, and the on‐treatment period was the time from first administration of the trial product to 2 weeks after the last dose for efficacy analyses, or 7 weeks after the last dose for safety analyses. Any off‐treatment time intervals (defined as ≥2 consecutive missed doses for efficacy analyses or ≥7 consecutive missed doses for safety analyses) were excluded from the on‐treatment period. Two estimands (treatment policy estimand and trial product estimand; supplementary materials [ p5 ]) were used to assess treatment efficacy and accounted differently for intercurrent events and missing data, as described previously. 11 , 12 The primary endpoints were analysed using a covariance and logistic regression model, as described previously. 11 Primary and confirmatory endpoints were part of statistical testing hierarchy, but supportive secondary endpoints were not. Results from statistical analyses are shown with two‐sided 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and corresponding p values. Additional details are available in the supplementary materials ( p5 ). 3 RESULTS 3.1 Baseline characteristics From 8 December 2020 to 23 August 2022, 351 participants from China were screened, of whom 300 were randomized 2:1 to receive either semaglutide 2.4 mg ( n = 195) or placebo ( n = 105) (Figure S3 ). This included 270 participants (90.0%) from mainland China and 30 (10.0%) from Hong Kong. In total, 292 participants (97.3%) were trial completers (semaglutide 2.4 mg, 97.4%; placebo, 97.1%). Of participants in the semaglutide group, 95.3% and 91.2% received a dose of 2.4 mg at Weeks 20 and 44, respectively (Figure S1 ). Overall, mean (standard deviation [SD]) body weight was 96.4 kg (17.4), mean waist circumference was 107.5 cm (11.1) and mean BMI was 33.8 kg/m 2 (4.6). Most participants (80.7%) had obesity, as defined by WHO criteria. A similar proportion of participants had T2D at screening between the treatment groups (semaglutide 2.4 mg 26.7% vs. placebo 24.8%). In participants with T2D, mean (SD) duration of diabetes was 5.7 years (4.9) and mean HbA 1c was 8.0% (0.7). The proportion of participants with prediabetes was also similar between groups (29.2% vs. 34.3%). Dyslipidaemia and metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) were the most reported comorbidities, affecting 63.7% and 58.3% of participants, respectively. In total, 260 (86.7%) participants had an FLI score ≥60 at baseline, and among these, 159 participants had an MASLD diagnosis (Table S1 ). Mean BMI changes from baseline at Week 44 were −4.0 kg/m 2 and −1.2 kg/m 2 with semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo, respectively (ETD –2.8 kg/m 2 ; 95% CI –3.5, −2.0; p < 0.0001; Table 2 ). A greater reduction from baseline to Week 44 in total cholesterol, very‐low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides was observed for participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group compared with the placebo group (Table 2 ). No changes in levels of high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol or free fatty acids were observed in either treatment group. Of the participants with an FLI ≥60 at baseline, scores improved to between ≥30 and <60 in 29.1% and 9.6% of participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo groups (OR 3.8; 95% CI 1.7, 8.6; p = 0.0010), respectively. Improvements to <30 were recorded for 19.0% of participants treated with semaglutide 2.4 mg and 4.8% of participants treated with placebo (OR 4.6; 95% CI 1.6, 3.6; p = 0.0054). The estimated mean changes in HbA 1c from baseline to Week 44 were −0.8% and −0.1% with semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo, respectively (ETD −0.7%; 95% CI −0.8, −0.5; p < 0.0001), and estimated change in FPG from baseline to Week 44 was −1.1 mmol/L (−18.9 mg/dL) with semaglutide 2.4 mg and −0.1 mmol/L (−1.4 mg/dL) with placebo (ETD –1.0 mmol/L; 95% CI –1.2, −0.7; p < 0.0001) (Table 2 ). Of the participants with prediabetes at baseline, 79.6% of the semaglutide 2.4 mg group achieved normoglycaemia by Week 44, compared with 25.0% of the placebo group (OR 11.7; 95% CI 4.2, 33.1; p < 0.0001), and 20.4% of participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group continued to have prediabetes versus 68.8% in the placebo group (OR 0.1; 95% CI 0.0, 0.3; p < 0.0001). Furthermore, no participants receiving semaglutide 2.4 mg progressed to having T2D, with 6.3% (two participants) in the placebo group progressing to having T2D. For the participants with T2D at screening, the observed mean changes in HbA 1c from baseline to Week 44 were −2.0% for semaglutide 2.4 mg and −0.6% for placebo. Additionally, the odds of achieving HbA 1c <7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or ≤6.5% (48 mmol/mol) were significantly greater with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo (Table 2 ). Most participants (semaglutide 2.4 mg, 61.5%; placebo, 57.7%) did not change their oral anti‐diabetes drugs (OADs) between baseline and Week 44. A greater proportion of participants who received semaglutide 2.4 mg decreased their OAD than those who received placebo (21.6% vs. 4.0%) (Table 2 ). Furthermore, no participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group increased their OAD medication compared with 20.0% in the placebo group. 3.5 Adverse events AEs were reported by 180/195 (92.3%) participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group and 87/105 (82.9%) participants in the placebo group (Table 3 ). The most frequently reported AEs were gastrointestinal (GI) disorders (semaglutide 2.4 mg, 64.6%; placebo, 33.3%). The most frequent GI disorders in the semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo groups were diarrhoea (28.2% vs. 6.7%) and nausea (20.5% vs. 4.8%) (Table 3 ). Most events were mild or moderate in severity, with the outcome reported as recovered or resolved (Table S4 ). The incidence of AEs was generally balanced between participants with and without T2D, although serious AEs (SAEs) were less frequently reported by those with versus without T2D (Table S5 ). Retinal disorder AEs for participants with T2D were reported in 11.5% of the participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group, with no events reported in the placebo group. The most frequently reported retinal disorder was diabetic retinopathy, with greater rates at baseline in the semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo groups (19.2% vs. 11.5%). Data on amylase and lipase levels are shown in the Table S7 . 3.5.1 Hypoglycaemia In participants without T2D, there was no difference in the proportion of hypoglycaemic events between treatment groups (semaglutide 2.4 mg, 4.2%; placebo, 3.8%). In participants with T2D at baseline (semaglutide 2.4 mg, n = 52; placebo, n = 26), one (1.9%) hypoglycaemic episode was classified as a severe or blood glucose‐confirmed symptomatic episode (<3.1 mmol/L [56 mg/dL]) in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group. 4 DISCUSSION This prespecified analysis of the STEP 7 trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of semaglutide 2.4 mg as an adjunct to lifestyle intervention in adults with overweight or obesity from China. The characteristics of participants in this analysis were similar to the overall STEP 7 population 11 ; however, compared with the STEP 1–4 trials, the STEP 7 Chinese population had more male participants (19.0–48.8% vs. 58.7%), lower BMI (35.9–38.4 kg/m 2 vs. 33.8 kg/m 2 ), smaller waist circumference (113.0–115.3 cm vs. 107.5 cm) and greater prevalence of comorbidities, in particular MASLD (5.7–21.6% vs. 58.3%). 13 , 14 , 15 Additionally, a global analysis of the incidence of MASLD found the presence of this disease in China to be consistent with the global incidence rate (29.2–32.5% vs. 32%). 16 Although this rate is not currently as high as some countries, including Turkey (48.4%) and the USA (47.8%), it is predicted that China will have the greatest overall increase in MASLD presence by 2030. 16 This prevalence of fatty liver disease complements data observed in a real‐world study of 15.8 million adults in China, in which 81.8% of participants with obesity were found to have this disease. 17 This highlights the need for effective management of overweight and obesity in China. In this analysis, an estimated mean reduction from baseline to Week 44 in body weight of 11.8% was observed with semaglutide 2.4 mg. This was consistent with the body weight reduction of 12.1% reported in the overall STEP 7 population, 11 and of approximately 10–16% up to Week 68 reported in previous STEP trials. 13 , 14 , 15 , 18 The beneficial effect of semaglutide 2.4 mg compared with placebo was generally seen across all subgroups (Table S3 ), which is consistent with STEP 1 and 2 responder analysis. 13 , 14 A body weight reduction of 5%–10% is recommended by Chinese guidelines for the management of obesity in adults. 19 In total, 85.4% of participants in the semaglutide 2.4 mg group in this analysis achieved a ≥5% body weight reduction from baseline. This is in line with the full population in the STEP 7 trial (85.3%), 11 and is broadly consistent with other STEP trials, including the STEP 6 trial in participants from East Asia. 18 In comparison with a similar population of Chinese adults, 58.2% of participants treated with the alternative GLP‐1RA beinaglutide achieved a ≥5% reduction in body weight from baseline over a 16‐week study. 20 Improvements in other cardiovascular risk factors were also observed with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo in this analysis, including systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, total cholesterol, very‐low density cholesterol and triglycerides. 20 Obesity can significantly affect various aspects of QOL, with several studies highlighting the correlation between increased obesity and decreased QOL. 1 , 21 , 22 In this analysis, the SF‐36v2 physical functioning score showed a significantly greater improvement with semaglutide 2.4 mg compared with placebo. These data align with results seen in the overall STEP 7 population, 11 as well as in an analysis of the STEP 1–4 trials. 23 No statistically significant difference was observed in the change in baseline IWQOL‐Lite‐CT physical function score to Week 44 between semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo. This is consistent with the results reported in STEP 7 11 and may reflect the fact that mean baseline IWQOL‐Lite‐CT physical function scores were greater than in STEP 1 and 2. 13 , 14 Therefore, participants may have had less scope for improvement. A greater proportion of participants treated with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo demonstrated improvements in FLI scores from baseline to Week 44, consistent with previous studies showing improvements in outcomes related to MASLD with semaglutide. 24 Irrespective of T2D status at baseline, treatment with semaglutide 2.4 mg improved HbA 1c , FPG and fasting serum insulin levels compared with placebo from baseline to Week 44. Of the participants who had prediabetes at baseline, a greater proportion treated with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo achieved normoglycaemia by Week 44. No participants receiving semaglutide 2.4 mg progressed to T2D. This generally aligns with results observed in many STEP trials, including the STEP 10 trial, which was conducted specifically in participants with prediabetes. 11 , 13 , 18 , 25 , 26 , 27 In our analysis, participants with T2D receiving semaglutide 2.4 mg had an improvement in HbA 1c of −2.0% over 44 weeks, while in STEP 2, which comprised of a population with T2D, HbA 1c improved by −1.6% over 68 weeks with semaglutide 2.4 mg. 14 Additionally, semaglutide 2.4 mg treatment increased the proportion of participants with T2D who achieved HbA 1c of <7% or ≤6.5% versus placebo; the odds of achieving HbA 1c <7% or ≤6.5% with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo was greater in this analysis (OR 21.2 and 20.6, respectively) than in the 68‐week STEP 2 trial (OR 10.9 and 9.8, respectively). 14 The majority of participants in the semaglutide group had successfully escalated to the 2.4 mg dose, indicating that semaglutide was well‐tolerated in this population. The AE profile in this population of Chinese participants was similar to that observed previously in the STEP trials (including STEP 7), and for the GLP‐1RA class in general. 28 No new safety concerns were identified. There was a greater incidence of AEs with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo, primarily attributed to GI AEs, although these were mostly non‐serious and reported as resolved or recovered. The proportion and rate of SAEs and AEs leading to discontinuation of the trial product were comparable between the treatment groups. As seen in the overall STEP 7 population, 11 there was an increase in rates of cardiovascular AEs for semaglutide 2.4 mg compared with placebo, of which palpitations were the most common. However, these events were primarily mild or moderate and considered to be unlikely to be related to the study drug. In participants with T2D, incidence of retinal disorders were higher with semaglutide 2.4 mg than placebo; the long‐term effects of treatment on diabetic retinopathy are being separately assessed. 29 Limitations of the study included a treatment duration of 44 weeks, restricting long‐term assessment in this population, and use of the WHO definitions rather than the Chinese‐specific BMI cut‐off values for overweight (≥24 kg/m 2 ) and obesity (≥28 kg/m 2 ). 2 Furthermore, there were insufficient numbers of participants on a dose of semaglutide <2.4 mg, so it was not possible to evaluate the efficacy of the lower dose of semaglutide (1.7 mg) in a Chinese population. Semaglutide 2.4 mg demonstrated statistically significant weight loss and cardiovascular risk factor benefits compared with placebo; however, this predefined analysis was not intended to establish superiority between groups. However, the STEP 7 trial was well‐conducted, as reflected by the high proportion of trial completers, including those who were on the trial product during the full 44‐week treatment period. Rates of missing data were low in both treatment groups, lending credibility to the observed results. 5 CONCLUSIONS In a population of Chinese adults with overweight or obesity, with or without T2D, treatment with once‐weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg as an adjunct to a reduced‐calorie diet and increased physical activity provided beneficial effects compared with placebo. These benefits included improvements in body weight loss, waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, lipids, glucose metabolism, MASLD, FLI scores, and SF‐36v2 physical functioning score. Furthermore, the AE profile was consistent with the GLP‐1RA class. These findings support a favourable benefit–risk profile of semaglutide 2.4 mg for weight management in this population.
